groups.issue: ungrammatical accepted answer 'She can cook very well biryani.'

flags.problem: acceptedAnswers includes 'She can cook very well biryani.' which is ungrammatical (adverb between verb and object).
flags.fix: Remove it; keep 'She can cook very good biryani.' (optionally add 'She can cook biryani very well.').

flags.problem: acceptedAnswers includes 'She can cook very well biryani.', which is ungrammatical (adverb between verb and object, the same kind of error as the frequency-adverb outcome).
flags.fix: Remove it; add 'She can cook biryani very well.' if wanted.

flags.problem: acceptedAnswers includes 'She can cook very well biryani.', which is ungrammatical (adverb between verb and object).
flags.fix: Remove it; keep 'She can cook very good biryani.'

groups.issue: key rewrites words outside the target; minimal correction not accepted

flags.problem: Key 'Last week we drank tea at that café every day.' changes 'the café daily' to 'that café every day'; the minimal correction 'Last week we drank tea at the café daily.' is not accepted.
flags.fix: Make the key 'Last week we drank tea at the café daily.' and add the 'every day' variant as an alternative.

flags.problem: The key changes words outside the target ('the café' to 'that café', 'daily' to 'every day'), so the plain correction 'Last week we drank tea at the café daily.' would fail an exact match.
flags.fix: Set the key to 'Last week we drank tea at the café daily.' (or rewrite the prompt more naturally).

flags.problem: The key 'Last week we drank tea at that café every day.' changes 'the café daily' to 'that café every day'. The correct minimal fix 'Last week we drank tea at the café daily.' is not in the key.
flags.fix: Make the key 'Last week we drank tea at the café daily.' (keep the other version only as an extra accepted answer).

groups.issue: text to the addressee keyed in third person / unnatural present; natural answers missing

flags.problem: Task is a text TO Hany but first accepted answer is 'I meet Hany at the café at six.' (third-person reference to the addressee); present simple 'I meet you at six' is unnatural for an arrangement, and natural answers ('I'm meeting you at the café at six', 'See you at the café at six') are absent. Same in B-9 and C-9.
flags.fix: Keep only 'you' variants, add 'I'm meeting/seeing/waiting for you ...' variants, and score word order with the 0/1/2 rubric rather than exact.

flags.problem: In a text to Hany, the key 'I meet Hany at the café at six' refers to the reader in the third person, and the bare present for a future arrangement is unnatural. The same applies to B-9 (Rasha) and C-9 (Mazen).
flags.fix: Make the key 'I'll meet you at the café at six.' Accept 'I meet you ...' and 'I am meeting you ...'. Remove the third-person versions, or state in the prompt that the text is a note about Hany.

flags.problem: The task is a text to Hany, but the accepted answers include 'I meet Hany at the café at six.' (third person, addressed to Hany himself). Under rubric §2.4 this does not do the task. The same applies to B-9 and C-9.
flags.fix: Remove the third-person versions, or reword the task as a diary note.

groups.issue: bare 'to'/'past' keywords accept answers with no time in words

flags.problem: Keyword list includes 'to' and 'past'; 'to' matches almost any sentence ('I go to bed...'), so the item is passed without writing a time in words. Same list in B-7 and C-7 (C-7 'go to bed' prompt makes it trivial).
flags.fix: Remove bare 'to'/'past'; require a number word (one..twelve) plus o'clock/past/to, or score with the rubric.

groups.issue: number-word keyword lists incomplete and different per form

flags.problem: Number-word keyword lists are incomplete and differ by form (A-8 lacks thirteen, fourteen, sixteen..nineteen, forty, sixty etc.; B-8/C-8 lack many numbers too), so correct answers score 0.
flags.fix: Accept any correctly spelled number word (pattern for one-ninety-nine + hundred) in all three forms.

flags.problem: The token list of accepted number words leaves out common prices (e.g. forty, sixty, seventy, eighty, hundred in A; one to four, six to nine and sixty+ in B/C), so correct answers may fail a key check.
flags.fix: Accept any correctly spelled number word, or list them in full (one to twenty, the tens, hundred).

groups.issue: C-5 is not a -teen spelling error

flags.problem: Slot 5 tests -teen spelling in A ('fivteen') and B ('forteen') but C uses 'nin' (nine), an easier, non-teen word; C-5 is not parallel.
flags.fix: Replace with a -teen error, e.g. 'The shop opens at ninteen minutes past eight' -> 'nineteen'.

groups.issue: f/v error tagged spelling_vowel

flags.problem: Tag spelling_vowel but 'fivteen' is a consonant (f/v) error; Arabic has no /v/, so the realistic Arabic-L1 confusion goes the other way (v written as f).
flags.fix: Retag (e.g. spelling_consonant) or use a vowel error like 'fiftin'.

flags.problem: 'fivteen', 'fivty' and 'forteen' are tagged spelling_vowel, but f/v confusion is a consonant/phonological transfer (Arabic has no /v/), not vowel omission.
flags.fix: Retag them as phon_f_v or consonant_spelling, or use vowel errors (e.g. 'sevnty', 'ninty', which are already used).

flags.problem: 'fivteen' (A-5) and 'fivty' (B-6) are f/v consonant errors but are labelled spelling_vowel. Arabic has no /v/, so learners usually write f for v, not v for f.
flags.fix: Relabel them (consonant spelling), or use vowel errors (e.g. 'fiftin', 'fourty') to match the label.

groups.issue: 'drinks soup' is acceptable English, so A-6 has no clear error

flags.problem: 'drinks his rice' (B-6) and 'drinks bread and cheese' (C-6) are not realistic Arabic-L1 errors; the real transfer is drink/eat with soup (Arabic 'yashrab shurba'). A-6 itself is weak because 'drink soup' is acceptable English from a cup.
flags.fix: Use realistic eat/drink transfer items (e.g. 'I drink a cigarette'->'smoke', or 'eat medicine'->'take'), and drop A-6 or accept 'drinks soup'.

flags.problem: 'My grandfather drinks soup every night' is acceptable English (soup is commonly drunk from a cup or bowl), so it is not a clear eat/drink error.
flags.fix: Use a solid food, e.g. 'My grandfather drinks bread with his soup.'

flags.problem: 'My grandfather drinks soup every night.' is acceptable English (soup can be drunk from a cup or bowl), so the planted error is not clearly an error, unlike B-6 (rice) and C-6 (bread). This also makes the forms unequal.
flags.fix: Use a food that cannot be drunk (e.g. 'drinks his beans').

groups.issue: statement stem ends with a question mark

flags.problem: Prompt 'I would like some orange ____ , please?' is a statement ending with a question mark: a model-error in the stem.
flags.fix: End with a full stop.

flags.problem: The prompt 'I would like some orange ____ , please?' puts a question mark on a statement.
flags.fix: End it with a full stop.

flags.problem: The prompt 'I would like some orange ____ , please?' ends with a question mark after a statement, so it is a faulty model sentence.
flags.fix: End it with a full stop.

groups.issue: 'small'/'little' also correct for a baby

flags.problem: 'The baby is not tall. She is ____' (short / small / little): 'small' is also correct for a baby, so the item has two right answers.
flags.fix: Change the subject to an adult ('My aunt is not tall. She is ____') or accept small.

flags.problem: 'The baby is not tall. She is ____ (short / small / little)': 'small' and 'little' are the natural words for a baby, so the item has three defensible answers.
flags.fix: Use an adult subject ('My grandmother is not tall. She is ____'), or change the distractors to non-height words.

flags.problem: 'The baby is not tall. She is ____ (short / small / little)': 'small' and 'little' are the most natural answers for a baby, but only 'short' is keyed.
flags.fix: Use an adult subject (e.g. 'My uncle is not tall. He is ____') or accept small/little.

groups.issue: slot 1 uneven: C-1 gives answer in stem + accepts 'boyish'; B-1 'bald' above A2

flags.problem: C-1 'she has a ____ haircut' with key 'short'/'boyish' repeats the word in the stem and uses a B2 word; A-1 'tall', B-1 'bald' (B1 in EVP) are not equal difficulty either.
flags.fix: Rewrite slot 1 with A2 words of equal difficulty in all forms (e.g. tall/short/fair) and drop 'boyish'.

flags.problem: 'Her hair is very short; she has a ____ haircut' asks for a word ('short') that is already in the prompt, and accepts 'boyish' (above A2). It does not measure the outcome and is much easier than A-1 and B-1.
flags.fix: Replace it, e.g. 'He has no hair on top. He is ____.' (bald), or a colour/hair-type cue.

flags.problem: C-1 gives the answer in the prompt ('Her hair is very short; she has a ____ haircut' with key 'short'). B-1 'bald' is EVP B1. A-1 'tall' is A1. The slot difficulties are very uneven.
flags.fix: Use the same kind of target in each form (e.g. tall/short/fair with an A2 context clue), and remove the giveaway.

groups.issue: kinship words above A1 / unequal across forms (sister-in-law, niece, nephew)

flags.problem: Slot 6 asks for 'sister-in-law' in C (B1 word, hyphenated) but niece/nephew in A/B; C-4 'niece' vs A-4 'aunt' / B-4 'uncle' is also harder (niece/nephew are A2).
flags.fix: Use kin terms of the same EVP level per slot (e.g. C-6 'The daughter of my uncle' -> cousin).

flags.problem: C-6 targets sister-in-law (EVP B1). A-6 and B-6 target niece and nephew, and C-4 targets niece. These are above A1, and B-4 (uncle) and A-4 (aunt) are easier than C-4 (niece).
flags.fix: Use A1 family words in all slots (aunt, uncle, cousin, grandparents), or match the word level across forms.

flags.problem: C-6 targets 'sister-in-law' (EVP B1), against 'niece' and 'nephew' in A/B. C-4 targets 'niece' against 'aunt' and 'uncle' in A-4/B-4. These are above A1 and not of equal difficulty.
flags.fix: Use A1 kinship words of equal level in each slot (e.g. aunt/uncle/cousin).

groups.issue: periphrasis 'the brother of my father' is grammatical; 's-genitive accepted so kin word not required

flags.problem: 'The brother of my father lives in Aswan' and the other periphrasis items (A-6, B-5, B-6, C-5, C-6) are grammatical English, not mistakes. Telling learners to 'find and correct the mistake' in a correct sentence is misleading, and the 's-genitive alternative shows the item does not force the target word.
flags.fix: Reword them as 'Write this with one family word: The brother of my father = my ___', or use real lexical errors (e.g. 'my uncle's son is my nephew').

flags.problem: Slots 5-6 correct 'The brother of my father' and similar. This is grammatical English, only less natural, and the key accepts "My father's brother", so the target word (uncle) need not appear. The items do not measure kinship vocabulary.
flags.fix: Key only the kinship noun (uncle/aunt/cousin/niece...), or turn the slots into gap-fills that require the word.

groups.issue: February harder to spell than August/September

flags.fix: Use months of similar spelling difficulty in all forms or put February in all three slot variants' distractor set.

flags.problem: 'May' is also correct in A-1, B-1 and C-1 but is not accepted.

groups.issue: normalise rule (case/punctuation ignored) defeats capitals-full-stops and day/month capitals

flags.problem: Rule 1 says capitals, punctuation and spelling of other words are always ignored, but for EN-F-A1-GR-capitals-full-stops and EN-F-A1-VO-days-months (e.g. 'tusday' -> 'Tuesday') the capital is the target or part of it; the rubric does not say whether a lowercase 'tuesday' scores 1.
flags.fix: Add an exception: when the targetForm is punctuation/capitalisation or a proper-noun spelling, case and full stops are scored.

flags.problem: Rubric rule 2 ignores case and punctuation, and rule 1 ignores capitals and punctuation. That makes every EN-F-A1-GR-capitals-full-stops item impossible to fail on its own target: 'ahmed lives in cairo' would match 'Ahmed lives in Cairo.' after normalising.
flags.fix: Add an exception: for outcomes whose target is mechanics (capitals-full-stops), and for the case part of days-months, do not normalise case or punctuation.

flags.problem: Rubric rule 2 says final and inner punctuation and case never change the score. Applied to EN-F-A1-GR-capitals-full-stops, the target form IS capitals and full stops, so every item in that outcome would score 1 for an unpunctuated, lowercase answer.
flags.fix: Add an exception to rule 2: for capitals-full-stops items (and any item whose targetForm is punctuation/case), case and punctuation are scored, not normalised.

groups.issue: 0/1/2 levels defined for grammar; vocabulary keyword items undefined

flags.problem: The 0/1/2 target_form rubric is defined for grammar forms; vocabulary free items store keyword lists in acceptedAnswers and the rubric does not say whether a keyword alone (wrong meaning, e.g. 'My grandfather is cheap') scores 2.
flags.fix: Add a vocabulary variant: 2 = target word used with correct meaning, 1 = right word with spelling slip, 0 = missing or wrong meaning.

flags.problem: The tf0/tf1/tf2 levels are defined for grammar forms. For the vocabulary free items (key such as 'classroom noun', 'clothing noun' or 'hair adjective + hair', with acceptedAnswers that are word lists) the rubric does not say what a slip is, whether a word missing from the list but valid counts, or whether a misspelt target word gets tf1.
flags.fix: Add a vocabulary variant: 2 = right word for the meaning, used in a sentence; 1 = right word misspelt or in the wrong form; 0 = no target-field word. State that the list is open, not closed.

flags.fix: Retype items 1-2 as multiple_choice and items 3-4 as controlled rewrite (short-answer).

flags.problem: Slots 1-2 are 'choose the correct sentence (a/b/c)' items but are typed gap_fill; slots 3-4 are word-ordering items typed multiple_choice.
flags.fix: Retype them (multiple_choice for 1-2, ordering/exact for 3-4).

groups.issue: slot-position choice typed gap_fill

flags.problem: Item types are mislabelled. Items 1-2 are 'which is correct' choices but are typed gap_fill. Items 3-4 are rewrite tasks but are typed multiple_choice (all forms). The same swap is in word-order-svo items 1-4 and frequency-adverbs items 1-2. The type decides how the grader maps the item (letter/text equivalence).
flags.fix: Retype items 1-2 as multiple_choice and items 3-4 as controlled rewrite (short-answer).

groups.issue: 'The the' accepted only in A-9 (key format differs)

flags.problem: A-9 lists 'The the' as accepted but B-9 and C-9 do not, so the key format differs across parallel forms.
flags.fix: Use the same acceptedAnswers pattern in all three forms.

groups.issue: 'a little room/clean/easy' not an Arabic-L1 pattern; B/C grammatical

flags.problem: 'it is a little room', 'it is a little clean' and 'it was a little easy', tagged lexical_opposite_negation, are not a documented Arabic-L1 pattern. 'it is a little clean' and 'it was a little easy' are also grammatical English, so B-5 and C-5 have no clear error.
flags.fix: Use documented errors, e.g. 'My baby sister is new' (already in slot 6) or 'This bag is not heavy, it is not heavy', or an Arabic-calque 'very much big'. Make sure the sentence is ungrammatical or semantically wrong.

flags.problem: 'Our house is not big, it is a little room' / 'a little clean' / 'a little easy' is not a documented Arabic-L1 pattern and is mislabelled 'lexical_opposite_negation'. A-5 also differs from B/C (noun phrase versus adjective).
flags.fix: Use a realistic error, e.g. using 'not' + adjective in place of the antonym when a contrast is required, or a known L1 opposite confusion (e.g. 'long' for 'tall', 'little' for 'young'). Keep the form parallel across A/B/C.

groups.issue: comparatives lighter/cheaper/shorter correct but not accepted

flags.problem: In the transfer items 'Box A is ____', 'Bag A is ____' and 'River A is ____', the comparatives 'lighter', 'cheaper' and 'shorter' are natural correct answers but are not accepted.
flags.fix: Accept the comparative forms, or change the prompt to 'Use the opposite adjective, not -er.'

groups.issue: accepted 'a big size' keeps the target error

flags.problem: The accepted answer 'This shirt is a big size for me.' does not fix the collocation error (the target is 'too big').
flags.fix: Remove that accepted answer.

flags.problem: The accepted answer 'This shirt is a big size for me.' keeps the error the item targets (big size for 'too big') with only an article added.
flags.fix: Remove it; accept 'too big' versions only.

groups.issue: B-4 tests be agreement, not vocabulary

flags.problem: 'How much ____ this jacket (is / are / cost)' tests be agreement, not clothes, colours or sizes vocabulary, while A-4 (try on) and C-4 (fit) test vocabulary. The forms are not parallel.
flags.fix: Replace it with a vocabulary choice, e.g. 'These shoes are too ____ (tight / short / young)'.

groups.issue: 'it is going to rain' correct but not accepted

flags.problem: For a forecast ('Take an umbrella, it is rain this afternoon') the most natural correction, 'it is going to rain', is missing, while 'it will rain' is accepted.
flags.fix: Add 'it is going to rain' and 'it's going to rain'.

groups.issue: '(It is on top.)' gives the answer away

flags.problem: The parenthesis '(It is on top.)' gives the answer away.
flags.fix: Remove it, or use a picture, or write 'The cat is ___ the table. It is not under it.'

groups.issue: 'near the station' accepted but does not name the place

flags.problem: 'near the station' alone is accepted for 'Where will they meet? (Write the place.)'. It does not name the place.
flags.fix: Remove 'near the station'; keep the answers that contain 'cafe'.

groups.issue: two-option yes/no items (50% guess)

flags.problem: Two-option yes/no items (PL-A1-RD-04 and PL-A2-RD-06) give a 50% chance of guessing right, which weakens placement decisions based on a few items.
flags.fix: Use 3-option or short-answer forms (e.g. 'Which day is the shop closed?').

groups.issue: distractor 'our' also correct (two right answers)

flags.problem: The options are his/our/their, and 'our' gives a grammatical, meaningful sentence in all three forms ('The twins love our grandmother', B: 'painted our classroom', C: 'fixed our garden gate'). That gives two correct answers.
flags.fix: Replace the distractor 'our' with one that does not fit (e.g. 'her' or 'its'), or add context that rules out 'our'. Apply to A-4, B-4 and C-4.

groups.issue: 'and' also correct; only 'but' accepted

flags.problem: There is no option list, and 'and' is also grammatical and natural ('I like tea, and my sister likes coffee'). The same applies to B-1 and C-1, but only 'but' is accepted.
flags.fix: Either add '(and / but / because)' with a context that forces contrast (e.g. '... but my sister doesn't'), or accept 'and'. Apply to A-1, B-1 and C-1.

groups.issue: 'a' also correct (referent not unique)

flags.problem: 'Can you open a window, please? It is hot.' is natural English, so 'a' is also correct. The same applies to B-2 ('turn off a light') and, less strongly, C-2.
flags.fix: Add context that makes the referent unique ('There is only one window in this room.'), or accept 'a'.

groups.issue: option 'the' also grammatical (two answers)

flags.problem: 'I have ___ apple in my bag.' with option 'the' is grammatical (a known apple), so there are two possible answers.
flags.fix: Replace 'the' with another distractor (e.g. 'some' or 'two').

groups.issue: 'teacher' is A1 vocabulary in an A2 item

flags.problem: 'A person who teaches is a ___ (teacher)' is A1 vocabulary (EVP A1). It does not separate A2 from A1 in an A2 band.
flags.fix: Use an A2 -er/-or noun (e.g. 'A person who visits a museum is a ___', or 'collects tickets', 'designs buildings').

groups.issue: free items key the given word; opposite not elicited

flags.problem: Slots 7-8 (all forms) ask for any sentence using a given word ('cheap', 'dirty'), with the word itself as the key. The outcome is giving the opposite; copying the given word shows nothing.
flags.fix: Ask for the opposite in context (e.g. 'Write one sentence about something that is not expensive.' and key 'cheap').

groups.issue: C-5 b/p spelling vs calques in A/B

flags.problem: C-5 'path room' is a spelling/phonology error (b/p), while A-5 and B-5 are lexical calques ('sleeping room', 'cooking room'). The slots test different things. The p-for-b direction is also the reverse of the usual Arabic-L1 substitution (b for p).
flags.fix: Use a calque in C-5 too (e.g. 'washing room'). Move any b/p item to a spelling outcome and use the b-for-p direction.

groups.issue: 'quarter to' harder than half/quarter past

flags.problem: 'quarter to' (C-3, C-9) needs counting back to the next hour and is harder than 'half past' (A-3) or 'quarter past' (B-3). Slot 9 has the same imbalance (A 'quarter', B 'half', C 'to').
flags.fix: Use the same time relation in each slot across forms (e.g. all 'quarter past' in slot 3 and all 'quarter to' in slot 9).

groups.issue: free prompts do not ask for 'going to'

flags.problem: The free items A-7 to C-8 ('Write one sentence about your plan for this evening') never ask for 'going to'. A correct 'I will...' or 'I'm meeting...' scores 0 under rule 3, so the score reflects the instruction, not ability.
flags.fix: Add 'Use going to.' to each free prompt.

groups.issue: free prompt does not ask for 'did'

flags.problem: The free items A-7 to C-7 do not ask for 'did'. 'Were you at home?' or 'Was it fun?' are correct past questions but would score 0.
flags.fix: Add 'Use did.' to the slot-7 prompts.

groups.issue: 'drinks his rice' / 'drinks bread' not realistic L1 errors

flags.problem: 'drinks his rice' (B-6) and 'drinks bread and cheese' (C-6) are not realistic Arabic-L1 errors; the real transfer is drink/eat with soup (Arabic 'yashrab shurba'). A-6 itself is weak because 'drink soup' is acceptable English from a cup.
flags.fix: Use realistic eat/drink transfer items (e.g. 'I drink a cigarette'->'smoke', or 'eat medicine'->'take'), and drop A-6 or accept 'drinks soup'.
